CausalChain: COL1A2 upregulation -> ECM remodeling -> Activation of integrin/FAK signaling -> Upregulation/activation of NXF1/THO complex -> Enhanced export of pro-angiogenic/metastatic mRNAs -> Accelerated liver tumor progression
Hypothesis: In liver neoplasms, the upregulation of COL1A2 induces significant extracellular matrix remodeling that activates integrin/FAK signaling pathways. This activated pathway, in turn, drives the upregulation and functional activation of nuclear mRNA export machinery—specifically NXF1 and key THO complex members. Enhanced export of mRNAs for proteins involved in angiogenesis and metastasis follows, thereby exacerbating tumor progression. By disrupting the COL1A2-integrin/FAK-NXF1/THO axis using state-of-the-art genomic and proteomic techniques (e.g., CRISPR interference, spatial transcriptomics), it may be possible to mitigate the export of oncogenic mRNAs and suppress tumor aggressiveness. This hypothesis refines the original concept by embedding COL1A2’s role within an integrin-mediated signaling framework to establish a mechanistic link between ECM dynamics and nuclear mRNA export.
Abstract: We hypothesize that in liver neoplasms, elevated COL1A2 expression drives distinct remodeling of the extracellular matrix (ECM) that activates integrin-mediated signaling, particularly through focal adhesion kinase (FAK). This signaling cascade upregulates and/or functionally activates nuclear mRNA export regulators such as NXF1 and components of the THO complex. As a result, these changes selectively enhance the export of mRNAs encoding key angiogenic and metastatic factors, contributing to aggressive tumor progression. To validate this mechanism, we propose utilizing advanced technologies including spatial transcriptomics, single-cell RNA sequencing, and CRISPR-based gene modulation to map the COL1A2-integrin/FAK-NXF1/THO axis in liver cancer. Our study aims to establish this integrative pathway as a novel therapeutic target, linking extracellular matrix dynamics directly to intracellular mRNA processing.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed that COL1A2 upregulation directly leads to ECM remodeling, which then modulates nuclear mRNA export factors (NXF1/THO complex), enhancing the export of oncogenic mRNAs and promoting tumor progression. The revised hypothesis retains these causal steps but incorporates a critical intermediate mechanism: integrin/FAK signaling. This addition clarifies how ECM remodeling is transduced into nuclear regulatory changes. Furthermore, contemporary technological approaches (spatial transcriptomics, single-cell RNA sequencing, CRISPR-based modulation) are suggested to validate and operationalize the hypothesis, thus bolstering both its novelty and practical viability.
